metadata.summary: Oncofetal programs are often co-opted in high-grade gliomas and represent tumor cell vulnerabilities for therapeutic exploitation. Here, we integrate single nucleus RNA-seq and single-cell ATAC sequencing data generated from germinal matrix and cortical plate regions macrodissected from prenatal and postnatal developing brain autopsy tissue, creating an expanded spatiotemporal multi-omic dataset of gliogenic progenitors. The integrated multi-omics data includes previously published data (Ramos et al, Nature Commun 2022; Herring et al, Cell 2022) as well as newly-generated and herein deposited data. We use this dataset to interrogate oncofetal cell state composition in grade 4 gliomas across several published high-grade glioma / glioblastoma (GBM) datasets to uniquely assess tumor heterogeneity related to infiltrative biology near the margin and disease recurrence, in addition to genomic drivers. Our analyses reveal the preferential enrichment of glial intermediate progenitor cell (gIPC)-like cell state in GBM, most reminiscent of third-trimester germinal matrix gIPC progenitors, across tumor regions and in recurrence, irrespective of EGFR amplification status.

metadata.summary: Microexons are extremely short exons that are highly conserved in vertebrates and are essential for normal brain development. Their small size poses a challenge for canonical exon-definition splice site recognition, which typically relies on spliceosomal interactions across standard length exons. Here, we determine the sequence and RNA structural features of neural microexons in humans in comparison with chickens. We find that neural microexons share intronic features that extend the functional distance between the branchpoint and the 3’ splice site, including distal positioning and lengthening of polypyrimidine tracts. Using experimental RNA structure-probing on a subset of neural microexons, we show that the branchpoint-to-splice site region is unusually accessible and relatively unpaired compared to other exon classes. However, we find little support for shared RNA secondary structures between orthologous human and chicken precursor RNAs despite high sequence conservation. Using the chick embryo as a developmental model, we demonstrate that a subset of neural microexons undergo dynamic, stage-specific regulation during brain development that correlates with expression of known microexon regulators, SRRM4 and NOVA1. Our data suggest that neural microexon splicing fluctuates during brain development and may rely on an extended polypyrimidine tract and structural accessibility for splicing efficiency, rather than conserved secondary structures.

observations.text: Congenital heart defects (CHD) arise in part due to inherited genetic variants that alter genes and noncoding regulatory elements in the human genome. These variants are thought to act during fetal development to influence the formation of different heart structures. However, identifying the genes, pathways, and cell types that mediate these effects has been challenging due to the diversity of cell types involved in heart development as well as the superimposed complexities of interpreting noncoding sequences. As such, understanding the molecular functions of both noncoding and coding variants remains paramount to our fundamental understanding of cardiac development and CHD. Here, we created a gene regulation map of the healthy human fetal heart across developmental time and applied it to interpret the functions of variants associated with CHD and quantitative cardiac traits. We collected multiomic data from 734,078 single cells sampled from 41 fetal hearts spanning post-conception weeks (PCW) 6 to 22, enabling the construction of gene regulation maps in 90 cardiac cell types and states, including rare populations of cardiac conduction system (CCS) cell types. We find that many such risk variants, both coding and noncoding, map onto gene regulatory networks in valve cells. In an unbiased analysis of 90 cardiac cell types and states, valvular interstitial cells (VICs) show the strongest enrichments for known CHD genes. Nine CHD genes are linked to common noncoding variants associated with other valve diseases or traits via transcriptional enhancers in VICs. CRISPRi experiments show that multiple CHD genes have cell-autonomous effects in VICs, including regulating the expression of other CHD genes and genes involved in cell migration and developmental patterning. Finally, we characterize a CHD-associated noncoding variant whose activity is specific to discrete structures within the heart, illuminating how such variants can impact specific aspects of heart structure and function. Together, these results suggest that genetic risk for many subtypes of CHD is influenced in part by genetic regulation of valvular cells, expanding our understanding of the cell types responsible for CHD beyond the working cardiomyocyte. This regulatory map of the human fetal heart provides a foundational resource for understanding cardiac development, interpreting genetic variants associated with heart disease, and discovering targets for cell-type specific therapies.

metadata.summary: Direct cardiac reprogramming relies on a combination of canonical cardiac transcription factors, typically consisting of Mef2c, Gata4, and Tbx5 (MGT). However, successful lineage conversion requires additional endogenous factors that coordinate the chromatin and transcriptional changes underlying fibroblast-to-cardiomyocyte conversion. Here, we identify Activating Transcription Factor 7 (Atf7) as a critical supporting factor that enables efficient direct cardiac reprogramming. Loss of function studies in primary murine cardiac fibroblasts demonstrate that Atf7 knockdown markedly reduces MGT mediated reprogramming efficiency, with the strongest impairment occurring when Atf7 is depleted during the early priming window of days 0–3. Transcriptomic profiling reveals that Atf7 knockdown disrupts the induction of cardiomyocyte gene programs while derepressing fibroblast  and extracellular matrix–associated pathways, shifting the global expression profile toward a non reprogrammed state. These findings support a bifunctional regulatory role of Atf7 in promoting cardiomyocyte-specific gene activation while repressing fibroblast-associated transcriptional networks.

metadata.summary: Myocardial infarction (MI) causes cardiomyocyte loss and fibrotic scar formation, disrupting electrical communication and impairing cardiac function. Conductive hydrogels have been studied to reconstruct an electroactive microenvironment for the infarcted myocardium, yet their regenerative effect is limited by the impaired function of surviving cardiomyocytes. Here, we developed a mechanoelectrically active and paintable hydrogel capable of converting cardiac motion into localized electrical stimulation to repair infarcted myocardium. The paintable nature of the hydrogel enables easy application onto irregular epicardial surfaces using a customized brush, while subsequent photocrosslinking allows selective adhesion of the hydrogel to only epicardial surfaces, not to surrounding tissues. Under cyclic loading and in contracting cardiac organoids, the hydrogel generated physiologically relevant electrical potentials, demonstrating efficient deformation-induced charge generation. In a rat MI model, the hydrogel providing electrostimulation alleviated ventricular wall thinning and fibrosis, promoted neovascularization and M2 macrophage polarization, and improved cardiac function. Transcriptomic analysis further revealed upregulation of genes involved in myocardial contraction and energy metabolism. As such, our study offers a minimally invasive and clinically translatable approach for cardiac repair and other tissue applications.

observations.text: Long COVID (LC) affects millions of individuals worldwide, particularly those with preexisting comorbidities. However, when assessing comorbidity-related risk factors for LC, it remains unclear whether preexisting comorbidities should be defined prior to SARS-CoV-2 infection or LC diagnosis. This methodological choice may substantially bias estimates of LC risk. In this study, leveraging Electronic Health Records (EHR) from 6,130,413 adults with documented COVID-19 across 49 U.S. states in the National Clinical Cohort Collaborative (N3C) from 2020 to 2024, we evaluated the impact of different comorbidity exposure-window definitions on LC risk estimates. We developed ensemble cross-fitted double/debiased machine learning to adjust for individual- and county-level confounders. We found that defining comorbidities before infection rather than before LC diagnosis yielded 8%-314% higher adjusted attributable risks and 3%-34% higher adjusted relative risks across 16 major comorbidities. Comorbidity-associated risks generally declined from 2020 to 2024, while substantial demographic, socioeconomic, geographic, and multimorbidity-related disparities persisted. Exposure-window specification can be a major source of bias in estimates of LC risk, particularly for comorbidities prone to delayed clinical recognition or underascertainment. More broadly, our results highlight how temporal misclassification of exposures in longitudinal EHR studies can distort risk attribution and population-level inference for risk stratification for LC and prioritization of prevention strategies in clinical medicine and public health, respectively.

metadata.summary: Ponatinib is a potent tyrosine kinase inhibitor and primarily used in the treatment of chronic myelogenous leukemia and Philadelphia chromosome-positive acute lymphoblastic leukemia. observations.text: Title and abstract screening is among the most labor-intensive steps of systematic reviews. Jev, a low-cost AI decision model, scores records against eligibility criteria without screening labels. We scored 169,982 records from 128 reviews and, after tuning on development reviews, evaluated 23 held-out reviews once and 31 Cochrane reviews post hoc. Jev outranked the best free ranker in all 23 held-out reviews (mean AUC 0.966 vs 0.831) and came within 0.011 AUC of Claude Opus 5.5 on 1999 records at about 1/700 of its list-price cost (US$0.02/1000 records). Combined with active learning, it raised work saved at 95% recall from 0.659 to 0.806. A fixed score threshold fell below 95% recall in 3 of 28 Cochrane reviews, whereas Jev ranking with statistical stopping (post hoc) reached 95% recall in all 51 reviews, reading 86-88% of records. Label-free ranking with Jev was accurate and inexpensive, but stopping safely required screening decisions.
observations.title: Label-free, low-cost AI ranking for systematic review screening

BackgroundIn people with type 2 diabetes (T2D), postprandial glucose weighs on glycaemic control, and carbohydrate counting is difficult. Patients can describe their meal but rarely quantify it.

ObjectiveTo assess (1) whether a small open large language model (LLM), fine-tuned on public data, estimates the carbohydrate content of a meal described in words, and (2) what this carbohydrate adds to the prediction of the postprandial glucose rise in two public cohorts.

MethodsStep 1: the Qwen3-4B LLM was fine-tuned with QLoRA on Nutrition5k dishes and compared with an automatically matched USDA food composition table and with Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B used without training, on test dishes (internal control) and on 100 real meals of ShanghaiT2DM patients, whose reference carbohydrate was computed from the recorded quantities. Step 2: the maximum glucose rise between 0 and 120 minutes ({Delta}Gmax) was predicted by personalised gradient boosting (M2), compared with a spline linear regression and with the Chronos-2 foundation model, using only information available at meal start and person-level cross-validation, in ShanghaiT2DM (people with T2D recruited in two Shanghai hospitals; carbohydrate estimated by the LLM) and CGMacros (free-living adults in Santa Barbara, California; carbohydrate entered in the dataset, no text). Step 3: the model was transferred between datasets. 95% confidence intervals (CI) were obtained by cluster BCa bootstrap (2,000 resamples).

ResultsOn the 100 real meals, the carbohydrate mean absolute error (MAE) of the fine-tuned model was 12.2 [9.9, 15.2] g, almost half that of the table (22.6 g; paired difference -10.5 [-16.8, -6.0] g) and nearly a third of that of the same model without fine-tuning (34.3 g), with a bias of -10.3 g; on test dishes it was 2.2 [2.0, 2.5] g. Personalised gradient boosting (M2) reached a correlation between predicted and observed rises of r = 0.63 [0.55, 0.69] in CGMacros (1,286 meals, 45 adults) and 0.49 [0.42, 0.54] in ShanghaiT2DM (2,339 meals, 99 people with T2D), about twice the linear reference (r = 0.32 and 0.23); for a rise above 50 mg/dL, its area under the ROC curve (AUROC) was 0.80 and 0.74, versus 0.64 and 0.68 with pre-meal glucose alone. Adding carbohydrate to pre-meal glucose changed r by 0.095 [0.068, 0.128] in CGMacros and by 0.004 [-0.010, 0.017] in ShanghaiT2DM; difference between datasets: 0.091 [0.060, 0.126]. Applied from one dataset to the other, the model lost correlation ({Delta}r = -0.11 [-0.17, -0.05] towards ShanghaiT2DM and -0.12 [-0.19, -0.04] towards CGMacros). The full "text [->] LLM [->] glucose" chain was evaluated in ShanghaiT2DM only.

ConclusionAn open 4-billion-parameter LLM, fine-tuned with QLoRA on public data and usable offline, almost halves the error of carbohydrate counting for real meals described in words compared with an automatically matched table, with an underestimation of large meals. Personalised gradient boosting, based on pre-meal glucose and the persons usual response, doubles the correlation of a linear reference for predicting the glucose rise in both cohorts. Carbohydrate improved this prediction in CGMacros but not in ShanghaiT2DM; the two datasets differ in many respects, and the cause of this gap is not established.

metadata.summary: Non-infectious granulomatous diseases, including sarcoidosis, lack targeted, steroid-sparing therapies to disrupt the persistent immune cell aggregates that drive chronic tissue morbidity. Integrating multi-organ single-cell RNA sequencing with spatial transcriptomics, we identify conserved macrophage-specific induction of osteopontin (OPN) across human skin, lung, and heart lesions. Mechanistically, we show that local tissue coagulation acts as a functional checkpoint, where proteolytic cleavage of OPN by tissue thrombin generates OPN fragments that activate macrophages through α4 integrin, which amplifies macrophage OPN expression and establishes a feed-forward circuit that sustains granuloma stability. In mouse models, genetic or pharmacologic disruption of this coagulation-immune axis, including the repurposed direct thrombin inhibitor dabigatran and thrombin cleavage-blocking OPN antibodies, reduces granuloma formation and promotes resolution of established chronic lesions. Together, these findings identify a thrombin-dependent feed-forward coagulation–immune circuit that maintains granuloma stability and provides multiple therapeutically actionable targets for non-infectious granulomatous disease.

metadata.summary: Truncating variants in desmoplakin (DSP) are a leading cause of arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy, a severe heart muscle disease characterized by fibrosis and life-threatening arrhythmias. Desmoplakin anchors the junctions that hold heart muscle cells together to the internal cytoskeleton, enabling the heart to withstand the force of each contraction. No targeted therapy exists, and DSP is too large for conventional gene replacement. Here we show, in explanted human hearts and in human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived cardiomyocytes, that truncating DSP variants reduce desmoplakin RNA and protein, and that the resulting haploinsufficiency renders cardiomyocytes vulnerable to cell–cell adhesion failure under contractile stress, preceded by disruption of the cell membrane. Lowering contractile force with the myosin inhibitor mavacamten prevents this failure. Circumventing the size of DSP, CRISPR-based transcriptional activation of the endogenous gene restores desmoplakin expression and rescues adhesion. Haploinsufficiency is therefore the primary defect in DSP cardiomyopathy, and transcriptional activation offers a therapeutic strategy.

metadata.summary: Myocardial ischemia-reperfusion injury triggers the recruitment of inflammatory cells, including neutrophils and monocytes. Currently, effective treatment strategies are not available for this widely occurring harmful condition. Using metabololipidomics, we uncovered relative reductions in the pro-resolving lipid mediator Resolvin-D1 (RvD1) early after reperfusion in both mouse and human transplanted hearts, and that exogenous treatment led to elevated tissue levels of RvD1. By intravital two-photon microscopy, we discovered that that pre-operative instillation of RvD1 into the donor heart or peri-operative systemic recipient RvD1 treatment reduced recruitment of neutrophils. Mechanistically, we found that RvD1 provides protection by signaling through Alx/Fpr2 on donor monocytes, which reduces their production of IL-1b, attenuating intravascular neutrophil aggregation and extravasation.  After allogeneic transplantation, peri-operative RvD1 treatment reduces myeloid cell recruitment, abrogates macrophage pro-inflammatory signaling within cardiac allografts, and significantly prolongs graft survival. This study defines the mechanistic basis of a therapeutic strategy that modulates inflammatory responses during myocardial ischemia-reperfusion injury and provides a platform for the design of clinical trials.

BACKGROUNDThe chromosome 9p21.3 locus is among the strongest genetic risk loci for cardiovascular disease (CVD), yet the regulatory mechanisms underlying this association remain poorly understood. Previous vascular disease studies focused predominantly on the role of this locus in smooth muscle cell (SMC) dysfunction, whereas its potential role in endothelial cells (ECs) remains less well characterized. Here, we sought to identify candidate regulatory variants at 9p21.3, their distal target genes, and effector transcripts that contribute to CVD-related phenotypes in ECs.

METHODSPromoter capture Hi-C was used to map chromatin interactions at 9p21.3 in primary human ascending aortic SMCs (n=6), supplementing the previously obtained ECs (n=16) dataset. To support the regulatory relevance of these interactions, expression quantitative trait locus analysis was performed in 136 vascular biopsies. Variant effects were prioritized in silico using AlphaGenome. The regulatory activity of the prioritized region was validated using CRISPR activation.

RESULTSChromatin interaction mapping identified a complex regulatory architecture at the 9p21.3 locus involving 19 putative regulatory elements and 15 genes across ECs and SMCs. MIR31HG showed the most recurrent distal promoter connectivity with the 9p21.3 region. Consistent with the chromatin interaction map, expression of MIR31HG transcripts was associated with genetic variation at the 9p21.3 locus. In ECs, the lncRNA MIR31HG, but not miR-31, was responsive to hemodynamic flow. Depletion of MIR31HG in ECs was associated with endothelial activation. Epigenetic tracks and deep learning predictions highlighted an active enhancer element at 9p21.3, which was subsequently validated by CRISPR activation and increased MIR31HG expression, confirming its capacity to regulate MIR31HG over a large genomic distance of approximately 538 kb.

CONCLUSIONSAltogether, these data implicate lncRNA MIR31HG as a likely effector of the 9p21.3 CVD locus, linking the cis-regulatory element and heritable genetic variation in the respective region to endothelial activation through long-range enhancer regulation.

metadata.summary: Diabetic cardiomyopathy is a clinical condition of ventricular dysfunction, with obesity and insulin resistance as the primary risk factors. Under this condition, the heart accumulates fatty acids and encounters lipotoxicity, which impairs cardiac insulin sensitivity and leads to cardiomyopathy. Angiotensin-(1-9) is a peptide of the counter-regulatory axis of the renin-angiotensin system with cardioprotective effects in myocardial infarction. However, its role in diabetic cardiomyopathy is unknown. To explore the role of angiotensin-(1-9), we first induced lipotoxic stress in the heart by high-fat diet (HFD) feeding in mice. Angiotensin-(1-9) was then administered for four weeks using osmotic mini-pumps. Cardiac function was assessed by, and insulin sensitivity was evaluated in tissues after a bolus of insulin injection. Moreover, lipotoxic stress in vitro was modeled by high glucose medium plus palmitate in neonatal rat ventricular myocytes (NRVMs). We show that angiotensin-(1-9) improves myocardial function and reverts pathological cardiac remodeling in mice. Moreover, angiotensin-(1-9) enhances whole-body glucose tolerance and reduces homeostatic model assessment of insulin resistance (HOMA-IR). We next demonstrate that angiotensin-(1-9) increases insulin sensitivity in the heart and skeletal muscle but not in adipose tissue or the liver. Mechanistically, angiotensin-(1-9) does not affect insulin signaling in cardiomyocytes at baseline, while it significantly improves insulin action under lipotoxic stress through AT2 receptor (AT2R) and PKA. These findings demonstrate that angiotensin-(1-9) improves cardiac function under metabolic challenge and promotes insulin signaling in cardiomyocytes under lipotoxicity, which may shed light on the therapeutic exploration against diabetic cardiomyopathy.

IntroductionThis study aimed to characterize the neurochemical profile of Alzheimers disease (AD) continuum stages using proton magnetic resonance spectroscopy (1H-MRS) data for brain metabolites and macromolecules. We used Orthogonal Projection to Latent Structures Discriminant Analysis (OPLS-DA) to classify diagnostic groups and assess feature importance.

MethodsOur dataset consisted of 7 T short-echo time 1H-MRS spectra of the posterior cingulate cortex/precuneus of individuals diagnosed with AD (n = 27) or Mild Cognitive Impairment (MCI, n = 27) and Healthy Controls (HC, n = 31). Classification used 100-round Monte Carlo cross-validation based on metabolite concentrations and macromolecular peak intensities. Variable importance in projection (VIP) was assessed across classification models to identify the most relevant neurochemical features. The resulting metabolite rankings were compared with previous literature to evaluate their biological plausibility.

ResultsClassification was strongest for AD versus HC (AUC=0.88) and lower for comparisons involving MCI. Metabolites contributing most strongly to classification included myo-inositol, ascorbate, and choline-containing compounds, consistent with previous studies on AD-related neurochemical alterations. In addition, specific macromolecular components were identified as relevant features, suggesting a potential contribution of MM signals to the characterization of AD-related neurochemistry.

DiscussionThese findings support the use of short-echo-time 1H-MRS as a complementary tool for characterizing neurochemical changes in the AD continuum, with potential applications in disease characterization and monitoring, warranting validation in larger cohorts.

observations.text: Metabolic networks are typically viewed as homeostatic systems that stabilize flux, energy charge, redox balance, and metabolite availability under perturbation. However, it remains unclear whether the same feedback architectures that support metabolic robustness can also generate learning-like, experience-dependent adaptation. Here, we develop a coarse-grained dynamical model of mammalian energy metabolism to test whether prior perturbation can improve future metabolic responses. The model represents core glucose, glutamine, fatty acid, and oxidative phosphorylation pathways as coupled ordinary differential equations with Michaelis-Menten-type fluxes, product-inhibition feedback, adaptive enzyme-capacity regulation, and explicit ATP costs for enzyme adjustment. Rather than aiming to reproduce quantitative fluxes for a specific cell type, the framework is designed to expose how metabolic feedback, regulatory cost, repeated perturbation, and environmental variability interact. We use this model to ask whether adaptive enzyme regulation enables improved recovery after repeated challenges, whether such effects depend on energetic control costs, and whether environmental variability broadens or constrains the set of reachable adaptive states. This approach provides a tractable way to investigate how homeostatic metabolic regulation may give rise to experience-dependent metabolic plasticity.

BackgroundUsing a population-based cohort from the Calgary Health Zone (CHZ), Canada, we integrated longitudinal antimicrobial susceptibility and prescribing data with the whole genome sequences of five major pathogens. We aimed to assess how antimicrobial resistance (AMR) responds to prescribing changes and determine which bacterial strains shape these dynamics.

MethodsWe analysed antibiotic prescribing rates, clinical and genomic data from 7,271 Staphylococcus aureus, 1,609 Enterococcus faecalis, 801 Enterococcus faecium, 11,363 Escherichia coli, and 2,319 Klebsiella pneumoniae isolates, associated with bacteraemia episodes in the CHZ between 2006-2022. Genomic clusters (referred to as strains) were identified using StrainGST and assigned to known sequence types (STs) or clonal complexes (CCs). Strain-level incidence, stratified by community-onset (isolates collected [≤]48h after admission) and hospital-onset (>48h after admission), AMR phenotypes, and prescribing rates were modelled using negative-binomial and binomial regression. Temporal trends were quantified using average annual percentage change (AAPC).

FindingsBetween 2010-2022, fluoroquinolone prescribing declined in both community (AAPC=-6{middle dot}8% [95% CI -8{middle dot}1, -5{middle dot}4]; p<0{middle dot}0001) and hospital settings (AAPC=-5{middle dot}1% [-6{middle dot}5, -3{middle dot}7]; p<0{middle dot}0001). This was accompanied by a significant reduction in fluoroquinolone resistance among Gram-positive species. Specifically, S aureus bacteraemia resistant to clinically important antibiotics, cloxacillin, ciprofloxacin, erythromycin, and clindamycin, declined from 2006 to 2022, mostly in hospital-onset cases (AAPC=-16{middle dot}0%, [-19{middle dot}3%, -12{middle dot}7%], p<0{middle dot}0001). In E coli, ceftriaxone and ciprofloxacin resistance were clustered in ST131 and the emerging ST1193; the latter increased steadily, particularly in community-onset cases (AAPC=17{middle dot}7%, [9{middle dot}0%, 30{middle dot}0%], p<0{middle dot}0001). CTX-M-27-producing E coli ST131 strains increased (AAPC=23{middle dot}8%, [17{middle dot}4%, 30{middle dot}5%], p<0{middle dot}0001) between 2008-2022, while CTX-M-14-producing E coli ST131 declined (AAPC=-15{middle dot}9%, [-21{middle dot}3%, -10{middle dot}2%], p<0{middle dot}0001) between 2013-2022. These trends were paralleled by an increase in community cephalosporin prescribing (AAPC=7{middle dot}3%, [4{middle dot}2%, 10{middle dot}5%], p<0{middle dot}0001) between 2010-2022. For K pneumoniae, hypervirulent ST23 was most common (N=88) with an increasing trend in incidence (AAPC=2{middle dot}3%, [-4{middle dot}4%, 9{middle dot}4%]) between 2006-2019.

ConclusionsThe contrasting resistance trends between Gram-positive and Gram-negative species underscore the complexity of AMR control efforts. Effective strategies will require stewardship efforts targeting multiple drug classes, genomic surveillance for emerging resistant strains, and interventions extending beyond hospital settings.

FundingThis study was funded by a Large Scale Applied Research Project competition award (2017) from Genome Canada, administered via Genome Alberta. IAL is supported by an Alberta Innovates Translational Health Chair and a UCalgary Research Excellence Chair, with additional support from the Canada Foundation for Innovation (CFI-JELF 34986), the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council (DG 04547). Microbial isolates were prepared for analysis at the Alberta Centre for Advanced Diagnostics, which is supported by PrairiesCan (000022734). This work was also supported by federal funds from the US National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases, National Institutes of Health, Department of Health and Human Services, under grant number U19AI110818 to the Broad Institute. JTS is additionally supported by the NIH/NIAID F32AI179151.

Research in contextO_ST_ABSEvidence before this studyC_ST_ABSWe searched PubMed for articles published in English up to Dec 23, 2025, using (antibiotic[tiab] OR antimicrobial[tiab]) AND (use[tiab] OR prescribing[tiab] OR consumption[tiab]) AND (resistance[tiab] OR "multidrug resistance"[tiab]) AND (relationship[tiab] OR association[tiab] OR correlation[tiab] OR effect[tiab] OR impact[tiab] OR influence[tiab] OR regression[tiab]) AND (genomic OR genetic OR ""molecular epidemiology) AND ("Staphylococcus aureus" OR "Escherichia coli" OR "Klebsiella pneumoniae" OR "Enterococcus faecalis" OR "Enterococcus faecium") NOT animal. This search yielded 739 articles.

Numerous studies have characterised the molecular epidemiology of these species over the past two decades:

For Staphylococcus aureus, extensive genomic surveillance has revealed that a limited number of sequence types have dominated global infections over the past two to three decades. Pandemic hospital-associated methicillin resistant S aureus (MRSA) strains such as CC5, CC22, CC80, and CC30 were widely established in the 1990s and early 2000s, often carrying large multidrug-resistant staphylococcal cassette chromosome mec (SCCmec) elements. Since then, community-associated MRSA strains, including ST8 (CC8, USA300), ST59, and ST80, have emerged and expanded, frequently harbouring SCCmec IV or V. Livestock-associated MRSA ST398 has also become widespread, particularly in Europe and North America. While vancomycin resistance in S aureus remains rare, reduced susceptibility has been reported sporadically, especially in ST5 and ST8. Overall, the distribution of S aureus sequence types continues to shift regionally, with the spread of community-associated strains into hospitals. These patterns largely reflect data from high-income countries whereas strain distribution tends to be more heterogeneous in low-and middle-income countries.

In Enterococcus faecium, genomic analyses have revealed a split population structure: clade A1 (clonal complex 17) comprises the vast majority of clinical, multidrug-resistant isolates, while clade B includes largely commensal, less drug-resistant strains circulating in the community. Globally, most clinical isolates now belong to clade A1 (CC17), which is characterised by near-universal ampicillin resistance, frequent vancomycin resistance, and additional resistance to aminoglycosides and fluoroquinolones. Since its emergence, CC17 E faecium has disseminated globally, with distinct subclones predominating in specific regions and time periods. In Europe and North America, ST17 and ST117 have become the predominant sequence types, commonly associated with vancomycin resistance and implicated in bloodstream infections. Although vancomycin resistance rates remain high in the USA and low in Canada, they have been relatively stable in recent years.

Genomic epidemiology has shown that Enterococcus faecalis is more genetically diverse than E faecium, with a highly recombinogenic genome and no clear separation into distinct clades. Early vancomycin-resistant E faecalis reports in the 1990s were sporadic and genetically diverse, but by the 2000s and 2010s, expansions of hospital-associated strains such as ST6, ST87, and ST179 became more prominent, particularly in Europe and North America, frequently producing beta-lactamase and exhibiting resistance to vancomycin, and high-level gentamicin.

For Klebsiella pneumoniae and Escherichia coli, studies have focused on the surveillance of extended-spectrum-beta-lactamase (ESBL) producing clones. The most common epidemic clones associated with multidrug resistance in E coli were ST131, ST1193, and ST69. The majority of ESBL-producing strains are attributed to CTX-M alleles with CTX-M-15 and CTX-M-14 being the predominant genotypes. Since 2000, the emergence of CTX-M-27, a single-nucleotide variant of CTX-M-14, has been increasingly reported. ESBL rates among hospital-associated E coli infections showed increasing trends in North America, Europe, and in many countries in Southeast and East Asia. ESBL rates varied considerably for K pneumoniae across different countries (15%-60%) with high rates primarily detected in Asia and in Southern and Eastern Europe. K pneumoniae bacteraemia was characterized by diverse strains with only a few associated with clonal outbreaks and hypervirulence, such as ST20, ST23, ST258, ST1.

Only one study has comprehensively integrated clinical, genomic, and antibiotic prescribing data. Pontinen and colleagues (2024) examined E coli bloodstream infections, showing that non-penicillin {beta}-lactam use influenced the success of widespread multidrug-resistant, extended-spectrum beta-lactamase (ESBL)-producing E coli clones. However, no previous study has combined longitudinal clinical, genomic, and antibiotic use data across multiple major pathogens.

Added value of this studyTo our knowledge, this study is the first to integrate longitudinal clinical, genomic, and antibiotic prescribing data for five key bacterial pathogens for an entire region over almost two decades. This combined dataset provides a unique opportunity to analyse the impact of changing antibiotic use on antimicrobial resistance trends across multiple organisms, as well as explore how pathogen-specific strains adapt to these changes over time.

Implications of all the available evidenceThis study underscores the critical importance of integrated, pathogen-specific surveillance programs for guiding antimicrobial stewardship. The observed association between declining fluoroquinolone prescribing and reduced resistance among Gram-positive pathogens illustrates the potential impact of targeted prescribing interventions. At the same time, the heterogeneous responses across bacterial species to this change in practice highlight that stewardship strategies must be tailored, rather than one-size-fits-all. Continuous genomic surveillance is essential for anticipating resistance shifts and enabling timely detection and response to emerging threats, particularly from high-risk clones with the capacity for rapid dissemination. Finally, reducing antimicrobial resistance will require an integrated approach with hospital-based interventions along with coordinated efforts in the community to limit transmission and overall antibiotic exposure.

metadata.summary: Background: Direct reprogramming of cardiac fibroblasts (CFs) into induced cardiomyocytes (iCMs) holds promise as a therapeutic strategy for heart regeneration. Post-myocardial infarction (MI), resident quiescent CFs (QCFs) activate and differentiate into myofibroblasts (MFs) in the infarcted region that drive pathological cardiac fibrosis. Converting these injury-activated MFs into iCMs could simultaneously alleviate fibrosis and replenish lost cardiomyocytes. However, whether the marked heterogeneity of CFs in the infarcted heart—and in particular the activation of QCFs into MFs—creates an intrinsic barrier that limits the reprogramming of these injury-activated MFs remains unknown. Methods: To define the molecular basis of this heterogeneity, we purified PDGFRα⁺ cardiac fibroblasts and used Postn lineage tracing to distinguish injury-activated MFs from quiescent CFs, enabling matched comparison of their reprogramming competence and single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) profiling of post-MI CF subpopulations. A targeted in vitro shRNA screen was conducted against 9 MF-enriched TFs as candidate molecular barriers for cardiac reprogramming. The lead candidate was validated in mouse MFs, QCFs, human iPSC-derived MFs, primary human cardiac fibroblasts, and in vivo using dual-recombinase-mediated lineage tracing. Mechanistic insights were gained through integrated bulk RNA-seq, scRNA-seq and Cleavage Under Targets and Tagmentation (CUT&Tag), together with functional assays including DNA-binding–deficient and domain-swap MEOX1 mutants. Results: We identified the upregulated transcription factor MEOX1—a known fibrosis determinant downstream of the key post-MI cytokines TGF-β1 and IL-1β—as the principal molecular barrier responsible for the profound reprogramming resistance of MFs. MEOX1 knockdown markedly enhanced reprogramming efficiency in both mouse and human MFs and enabled GATA4-free reprogramming combinations. This inhibition depended on MEOX1’s transcriptional activation activity, as disrupting its DNA-binding domain or fusing it to a repressor domain rescued reprogramming. Integrated scRNA-seq and CUT&Tag analyses revealed that MEOX1 binds and stabilizes a fibrotic, MF-defining transcriptional program that antagonizes the cardiogenic program, while also modulating the inflammatory response; its knockdown disrupted this fibrotic network to favor iCM fate acquisition. Using stringent dual-recombinase lineage tracing, we demonstrated that MEOX1 knockdown enables highly efficient in vivo MF-to-iCM conversion, leading to significant reductions in cardiac fibrosis and substantial improvement in cardiac function after MI. Conclusions: Our study identifies the pathological upregulation of MEOX1 as a key mechanism underlying the reprogramming resistance of post-MI MFs, in both mouse and human. Overcoming this barrier achieves unprecedented, lineage-confirmed in vivo reprogramming efficiency, thereby addressing a significant obstacle for the clinical translation of in situ reprogramming therapies. Data included in this Series comprise the original bulk RNA-seq datasets of MGTM-reprogrammed mouse cardiac fibroblasts with control or Meox1 knockdown and with control vector/GFP or MEOX1 overexpression; RNA-seq datasets from human iPSCs, iPSC-derived cardiac fibroblasts, and iPSC-derived myofibroblasts; scRNA-seq datasets from MGTM-induced iCM cultures and normal or day-3 post-MI mouse hearts; MEOX1 CUT&Tag data; and the newly added three-biological-replicate bulk RNA-seq dataset comparing MGTM + shCtrl with MGTM + shMeox1 used for the revised manuscript.

Disability is an important population-health concern, but adult-specific evidence on its distribution and socioeconomic patterning remains limited in Somaliland. This study estimated the prevalence and distribution of reported disability among adults in Somaliland and examined socioeconomic inequality, reported mental/psychological illness, and their co-occurrence.

We conducted a cross-sectional secondary analysis of the 2020 Somaliland Health and Demographic Survey. The analysis included 14,579 adults aged >18 years who were usual residents, had the disability module administered, and had a defined reported mental/psychological illness measure. Reported disability was defined as at least one positive response across seven disability domains: sight, hearing, speech, learning, mobility, self-care, and mental. Survey-weighted prevalence estimates and design-based comparisons were calculated. Survey-weighted logistic regression assessed associations with household wealth and other covariates. Socioeconomic inequality was assessed using a concentration index and the normalized Erreygers concentration index. Co-occurrence was evaluated by comparing observed joint prevalence with that expected under statistical independence and by survey-weighted logistic regression.

The survey-weighted prevalence of any reported disability was 7.30% (95% CI 6.65-8.02). Sight was the most frequently reported domain (3.83%, 95% CI 3.19-4.59), followed by hearing (1.54%, 95% CI 1.20-1.97) and mobility (1.39%, 95% CI 1.14-1.70). Disability prevalence increased markedly with age, from 4.15% among adults aged 18-29 years to 23.96% among those aged >60 years. The crude wealth pattern was non-monotonic and was not statistically detectable after adjustment for residence and region. The concentration index for reported disability was 0.0584 (SE 0.0284, p=0.0415). Reported mental/psychological illness had a weighted prevalence of 0.71% (95% CI 0.50-1.00). Both reported disability and reported mental/psychological illness occurred in 0.5032% of adults, compared with 0.05185% expected under statistical independence; the observed-to-expected ratio was 9.70 (95% CI 7.60-11.81). After adjustment for age group and sex, reported disability was strongly associated with reported mental/psychological illness (OR 42.99, 95% CI 18.45-100.18).

Reported disability affected approximately one in fourteen adults in Somaliland and showed a marked age gradient and substantial geographic variation. The crude socioeconomic pattern was attenuated after adjustment for geographic context, while concentration analysis indicated modest marginal concentration toward higher wealth ranks. Reported mental/psychological illness was uncommon but co-occurred with reported disability more often than expected under independence. These findings provide an adult population baseline for Somaliland while highlighting the need to distinguish survey-reported disability from the separate mental/psychological illness construct and to interpret the findings within the limitations of cross-sectional, survey-reported measures.

Background & AimsLanguage development in autism is heterogeneous and strongly predicts later functioning. The balance between receptive and expressive abilities and their developmental trajectories, however, remains poorly understood. While some autistic children exhibit a relative expressive advantage (ExpAdv), others show receptive advantage (RecAdv) or a balanced profile. Prior studies report inconsistent findings and are often limited by cross-sectional designs and small samples. The present study aimed to (1) describe longitudinal trajectories of receptive and expressive language in autistic and typically developing (TD) children; (2) classify children into ExpAdv, Balanced, and RecAdv profiles across early childhood; and (3) examine the stability and transitions of these profiles over time, including associated clinical features.

MethodsWe analyzed 1,174 longitudinal time points from 318 autistic children and 294 time points from 108 TD children (1.2-5.8 years) from the Geneva Autism Cohort. Receptive and expressive language were assessed with the Mullen Scales of Early Learning. Receptive-expressive balance was quantified as the ratio of receptive to expressive age equivalent scores, classifying children into ExpAdv, Balanced, and RecAdv profiles using adapted cut-offs. Mixed-effects models examined developmental trajectories, and Sankey diagrams visualized profile transitions. Autism features and adaptive behavior were compared across profiles.

ResultsAutistic children displayed lower expressive and receptive language than TD peers, with receptive abilities exceeding expressive skills in both groups. Overall, 30-35% of autistic children were classified as ExpAdv at 18-36 months, declining to [~]12% by 48-54 months, while Balanced and RecAdv profiles became more prevalent with age. ExpAdv was associated with slower verbal and non{-}verbal developmental gains. Balanced and RecAdv profiles showed moderate stability (50-60%), whereas ExpAdv was less stable and frequently transitioned toward Balanced profiles. Autistic children with stable ExpAdv profiles were more often female and showed weaker adaptive communication.

ConclusionsReceptive-expressive language profiles in autistic children are dynamic. ExpAdv profile is more frequent in younger autistic children, less stable, and linked to slower verbal and non-verbal development and greater autism severity.

ImplicationsExpAdv may represent an early marker of autism associated with slower expressive and receptive language growth. Longitudinal monitoring of receptive and expressive skills is essential, as transitions toward Balanced or RecAdv profiles are associated with improved developmental outcomes. We discuss clinical considerations regarding language assessment, longitudinal monitoring, and interpretation of receptive-expressive profiles.

observations.text: Clustering is a fundamental task in data analysis: grouping similar objects together into distinguishable subsets. Here, we introduce HDCluster, a novel high-degree graph-based clustering algorithm designed to effectively and rapidly handle various real-world clustering applications, particularly in the context of super-resolution single molecule localization microscopy (SMLM). HDCluster efficiently handles datasets with large and variable numbers of clusters, without requiring prior knowledge of the cluster count, relying on only one parameter. The high speed and efficiency of HDCluster allow it to handle large SMLM datasets with millions of localizations. A comprehensive quantitative comparison shows that HDCluster is equivalent to state-of-the-art clustering methods based on clustering performance measures, such as ARI and AMI, on simulated datasets. In terms of time efficiency, HDCluster significantly outperforms other clustering algorithms on large DNA-PAINT datasets. metadata.summary: Nuclear receptor subfamily 4 group A member 2 (NR4A2) is a widely expressed immediate early gene induced by a host of physiological signals such as growth factors, cytokines, and neurotransmitters. In the adult mammalian heart, including in cardiomyocytes, NR4A2 mRNAs increase more than 60-fold in response to beta-adrenergic stimulation. However, the nature of the transcriptional remodeling induced by NR4A2 in the stressed heart has remained poorly investigated. We show here that NR4A2 activation in mouse cardiomyocytes leads to a rapid remodeling of the cardiac microRNA network. A total of 35 miRNAs were down-regulated, including the muscle-specific miR-133a and miR-499. On the opposite, 65 miRNAs were up-regulated, with a strong representation of miRNAs encoded within the imprinted Dlk1-Dio3 domain. Non-coding RNAs from the Dlk1-Dio3 locus are known for coordinating critical steps of cardiac development such as cardiac lineage commitment, cardiac morphogenesis, and cardiomyocyte proliferation, and for inhibiting mitochondrial function in myocytes. The findings shed light on a novel regulatory mechanism controlling cardiac homeostasis, and establish a framework to investigate further the roles played by NR4A2 in cardiac adaptation or maladaptation to various acute and pathological stress conditions.

observations.text: The traditional scoring functions for protein-ligand binding affinity prediction usually adopt fixed mathematical formulas to characterize atomic interaction energies, where electrostatic interactions are described by the a/r function and van der Waals interactions by the b/r^6 -c/r^12 function. These fixed power exponents of distance-based variables severely limit the predictive flexibility and generalization of conventional scoring models. To address this limitation, this study proposes an improved prediction strategy with unrestricted power exponents for distance-dependent atomic interaction variables. To explore the upper boundaries of the predictive powers, the optimized distance-based descriptors were integrated with linear regression and artificial neural network algorithms to construct novel models for protein-ligand binding affinity and binding energy prediction. All linear, artificial neural network, and hybrid models in this work were trained and validated on the latest high-quality dataset from PDBbind (version 2024). Quantitative evaluation based on the Pearson's correlation coefficient (R) demonstrated that the optimized linear models achieved a moderate predictive performance with R values ranging from 0.700 to 0.800 on the high-quality affinity dataset, while the artificial neural network-based hybrid models yielded substantially improved accuracy, with R values between 0.800 and 0.900. Comparative analysis verified that the optimal models established in this study outperform previously-reported state-of-the-art linear and machine learning-based scoring functions. Specially, this work indicates that the scoring functions with explicit mathematical expressions can achieve a high accuracy close to the experimental error for affinity prediction in a dataset composed of several thousand protein-ligand complexes. The overall results indicate that rationally-optimized power exponents for distance-based variables can effectively enhance the predictive accuracy of protein-ligand binding affinity prediction, providing a reliable and efficient tool for computational drug discovery.
observations.title: Exploring the Upper Boundaries of Distance-Based Protein-Ligand Binding Affinity Prediction: Accuracy Improvements via Linear Regression and Artificial Neural Networks

metadata.summary: Degenerative mitral valve disease (DMVD) is a highly prevalent cardiac condition characterized by mitral valve interstitial cell (MVIC) activation and extracellular matrix (ECM) remodeling. To investigate the transcriptional reprogramming underlying these processes, we performed RNA sequencing on an established three-dimensional (3D) porcine MVIC-collagen (VIC-COL) model.Following a 14-day maturation period, the constructs were treated with transforming growth factor-β1 (TGF-β1) for an additional 14 days, while untreated constructs cultured for the same duration served as controls. Samples were prepared from cells derived from three independent biological replicates (i.e. mitral valves from three different pigs). For each replicate, three constructs were pooled as one sample for final analysis. The analysis identified 915 differentially expressed genes (DEGs), revealing a significant transcriptional shift. Specifically, TGF-β1 led to a predominant upregulation of immune and inflammatory networks, including the IL-6/JAK/STAT3, TNF-α/NF-κB, and NOD-like receptor pathways, alongside processes associated with extracellular matrix organization, cell-cell adhesion, cell adhesion regulation, and cellular senescence. Furthermore, cross-species transcriptomic comparisons with a clinical canine DMVD dataset confirmed the conservation of these immune-centric signatures. Collectively, our findings suggest that immune-inflammatory signaling may act as a key modulator of ECM remodeling associated with MVIC activation. Moreover, the 3D VIC-COL system established in this study can serve as a reliable in vitro platform for investigating MVIC activation, ECM remodeling, and immune-related pathway changes in DMVD pathogenesis.

metadata.summary: Truncating variants in desmoplakin (DSP) are a leading cause of arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy, a severe heart muscle disease characterized by fibrosis and life-threatening arrhythmias. Desmoplakin anchors the junctions that hold heart muscle cells together to the internal cytoskeleton, enabling the heart to withstand the force of each contraction. No targeted therapy exists, and DSP is too large for conventional gene replacement. Here we show, in explanted human hearts and in human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived cardiomyocytes, that truncating DSP variants reduce desmoplakin RNA and protein, and that the resulting haploinsufficiency renders cardiomyocytes vulnerable to cell–cell adhesion failure under contractile stress, preceded by disruption of the cell membrane. Lowering contractile force with the myosin inhibitor mavacamten prevents this failure. Circumventing the size of DSP, CRISPR-based transcriptional activation of the endogenous gene restores desmoplakin expression and rescues adhesion. Haploinsufficiency is therefore the primary defect in DSP cardiomyopathy, and transcriptional activation offers a therapeutic strategy.

Background and AimsArtificial intelligence (AI) may help differentiate Takotsubo syndrome from acute anterior ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) on electrocardiograms (ECGs). We developed an ECG image-based model and evaluated whether AI assistance and visual explanations improved reader performance, overall and by reader background.

MethodsA self-supervised three-architecture deep learning ensemble was developed and externally validated using 12-lead ECG images from two institutions, recorded [≤]14 days after onset regardless of reperfusion. A four-phase reader study compared unaided interpretation, a reference sheet, and AI assistance (Phases 1-3). In Phase 4, readers were randomized to the reference sheet alone, AI predictions, or predictions with gradient-weighted class activation mapping (Grad-CAM). Correctness was analyzed with generalized linear mixed-effects models.

ResultsCohorts comprised 832 development and 95 external validation participants. External validation accuracy was 0.914, and the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve was 0.970 (95% CI, 0.938-0.992), or 0.958 using first recorded ECGs. Among 70 readers, the estimated probability of correct diagnosis increased from 0.632 unaided to 0.864 with AI (odds ratio [OR], 3.71; P<0.001). In Phase 4, AI assistance improved accuracy vs reference sheet (OR, 4.28; 95% CI, 3.08-5.95), and Grad-CAM added value (OR, 1.53; 95% CI, 1.04-2.25). In exploratory analyses, less experienced readers gained more; with AI, non-cardiologists outperformed cardiologists. Mean AI-assisted reader accuracy remained below model accuracy.

ConclusionsAn ECG image-based ensemble differentiated Takotsubo syndrome from anterior STEMI and improved reader performance, particularly with visual explanations. Experience-related differences emphasize the need for effective human-AI interaction.

observations.text: Transcript-based de-identification protects textual records but leaves sensitive health information (SHI) directly audible in source recordings, limiting trustworthy reuse of clinical audio. However, standardized evaluations of recording-level SHI detection remain limited. We established the SREDH-AICUP 2025 benchmark to evaluate recording-level SHI detection systems and characterize the approaches. All 22 qualifying systems combined automatic speech recognition with downstream SHI detection, whereas we additionally evaluated end-to-end detection from audio. Pipeline baselines outperformed the end-to-end baseline in transcription (MER, 0.123 vs 0.155) and SHI detection (macro-F1, 0.507-0.653 vs 0.422). Synthetic Mandarin speech-text augmentation enabled the end-to-end model to detect Mandarin SHI that was not identified without augmentation (macro-F1, 0.171 vs 0). Foundation models showed category-specific differences in SHI recognition, and type-aware adaptive routing improved macro-F1 from 0.656 to 0.697. These findings establish standardized reference performance, characterize current system designs, and demonstrate how language-specific augmentation and category-aware model integration can improve recording-level SHI detection.

observations.text: Integrative macromolecular docking pipelines generate thousands of candidate structural decoys, relying on downstream pairwise ensemble analysis, including Root-Mean-Square Deviation (RMSD) matrices and Fraction of Common Contacts (FCC) clustering, to identify biologically relevant binding poses. However, pairwise structural comparisons scale quadratically (O(N^2)), and canonical workflows in HADDOCK3 historically rely on disk-bound trajectory serialization and iterative CPU set operations, creating a quadratic computational and storage bottleneck for large ensembles. Here, we demonstrate that these operations can be reformulated as continuous linear algebra on GPU-resident tensors: structural superposition via batched Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) and residue contact overlap via binary matrix multiplication (M = A A^T). Across empirical benchmarks spanning N = 200 to 10,000 models (evaluating up to 49,995,000 decoy pairs), our GPU implementation achieves a 6.41-fold compute speedup on Apple Silicon (MPS) and up to 12.2-fold end-to-end acceleration in an N = 5,000 ablation on NVIDIA CUDA by eliminating trajectory disk I/O. Crucially, the implementation achieves zero downstream structural regression relative to canonical baselines, preserving identical cluster assignments (Adjusted Rand Index ARI = 1.0000, zero differing assignments) with sub-microangstrom RMSD concordance (Delta_max <= 4.07 x 10^-7 Angstrom on single-precision MPS; machine-precision Delta_max <= 8.88 x 10^-16 Angstrom on double-precision CUDA). The accelerated code, test suites, and benchmarking workflows are openly accessible on GitHub under the Apache-2.0 license.
